items.prompt: White's rook has just gone from a1 to a2, and Black's king from e8 to d8. It is White's turn: put the rook back on the square it came from.

claims.statement: The rook can go back to a1.
The white rook stands on a2.

hints: The rook came from the first row.
It moves along the a-file, one square down.
Undo the rook's last step.
items.explain: The rook slides one square down the a-file, back to a1. Black's king is on d8 now, not e8, so the position has not quite come back yet; one more move by Black would do it.

feedback_by_move.a2a8: The rook goes to the far end of the file. That is a new square, so nothing comes back.

items.prompt: This position (White to move) has now appeared twice: once at the start of the shuffle and once after the rook and the king went out and back. May White claim a draw by repetition now?

claims.statement: The game is still going on: no checkmate, no stalemate, no check.
The move is legal here.

hints: How many appearances does the rule ask for?
Count the start as the first appearance.
Two appearances are one short.
items.explain: Not yet. A claim needs the third appearance. The start was the first, this is the second, so one more round of the same moves would make three.

items.prompt: The pieces have just returned to their starting squares, but this time it is Black's turn to move. Is this the same position as the start, where White was to move?

claims.statement: The white rook is back on a1.
The black king is on e8.
Black is the one to move: the black king can step to d8.

hints: Look at the squares first, then ask whose turn it is.
The start had White to move.
A different player to move means a different position.
items.explain: No. The pieces stand on their starting squares, but a position also includes whose turn it is. Here Black moves; at the start White moved. So these are two different positions.

items.prompt: White's rook went out to h2 and came back to h1. Tap every square White's king can move to.

claims.statement: The king can go to exactly d1, d2, e2, f1 and f2.
Castling (the king to g1) is not allowed here.

hints: A king moves one step in any direction.
Empty squares next to the king are open, unless attacked.
Castling would put the king on g1. Is that allowed after the rook has moved?
items.explain: The king can step to any of five empty neighbouring squares. It cannot castle: the rook left its corner once, and that ends the right to castle on that side for good, even though the pieces look as they did.

items.prompt: Here a queen and a king play against a king (White to move). Each side steps out and back twice, in the same way. Counting the start, how many times has this position appeared?

claims.statement: The game is still going on: no checkmate, no stalemate, no check.
The queen can step to g3.

hints: Count the start as appearance number one.
Each out-and-back round brings the position back once.
Two rounds, plus the start.
items.explain: Three. The start is the first appearance, each of the two rounds brings it back once more, so White may now claim a draw.

items.prompt: Black has just pushed a pawn, so the clock read 0. Since then: a white king move, a black king move, and now a white bishop move that gives check. What does the clock read?

claims.statement: Black is in check.
The white bishop stands on b5.

hints: Count the half-moves since the pawn push, both players.
The last one is the check.
A check does not reset anything.
items.explain: Three half-moves have passed since the pawn push: a king move, a king move and the bishop's check. The check does not reset the count.

items.prompt: The clock reads 37. White's rook takes the knight on h1. Does this move send the clock back to zero?

claims.statement: The rook can take on h1.
A black knight stands on h1, so the move is a capture.

hints: What does the rook do to the knight?
Is a piece removed from the board?
Captures change the game for good.
items.explain: Yes. A capture removes a piece for good, so the count of half-moves without progress starts again from zero.

items.prompt: The clock reads 37. White's rook goes to a8, giving check. Does this move send the clock back to zero?

claims.statement: The rook can go to a8.
After the move the black king is attacked, so it is a check.

hints: Is anything captured?
Did a pawn move?
A check feels forcing, but only captures and pawn moves reset the count.
items.explain: No. The move is a check, but nothing is captured and no pawn moves, so the clock only goes up, to 38.

items.prompt: The clock reads 37. White's king steps from d2 to e2. Does this move send the clock back to zero?

claims.statement: The king can step to e2.
After the move the black king is not attacked.

hints: Is anything captured?
Did a pawn move?
A quiet king step is just one more half-move.
items.explain: No. A quiet king step captures nothing and moves no pawn, so the clock goes up to 38.

items.prompt: The clock reads 60 and it is Black's turn. Black pushes the pawn from e7 to e5. Does this move send the clock back to zero?

claims.statement: The pawn can jump to e5.
A black pawn stands on e7.

hints: Which piece moves?
Pawns cannot go backwards.
Every pawn move changes the game for good.
items.explain: Yes. A pawn can never move back, so any pawn move, even a quiet one, sends the count back to zero.

items.prompt: The clock reads 100 half-moves, with no capture and no pawn move, and it is White's turn. May White claim a draw?

claims.statement: The game is still going on: no checkmate, no stalemate, no check.
The move is legal here.

hints: What number does the rule ask for?
100 half-moves is fifty moves by each player.
The clock has reached the number.
items.explain: Yes. A hundred half-moves with no capture and no pawn move allow a claim. White is a rook ahead, so claiming would be a poor choice, but the rule allows it.

items.prompt: The clock reads 98 half-moves, and it is White's turn. May White claim a draw by the fifty-move rule now?

claims.statement: The game is still going on: no checkmate, no stalemate, no check.
The move is legal here.

hints: What number does the rule ask for?
98 is two short of fifty moves each.
Two more half-moves are needed.
items.explain: Not yet: two half-moves are missing. At 100 the claim is allowed.

items.prompt: White is behind: three black rooks against one white queen. Can White save the game by checking again and again?

claims.statement: The engine (a chess program) rates the position as level, depth 16.
After the queen checks on e8 it also covers g8, so the king's only free square is h7.

hints: Look at where Black's king can run after a check.
The queen checks along the last row, then along a diagonal.
The king has only two squares and the queen can keep switching checks.
items.explain: Yes. The queen checks on e8, the king has only h7, the queen checks along the diagonal, and the king goes back. The queen can repeat this, so the chess program rates the position as level despite the extra rooks.

items.prompt: Same idea, one change: a black bishop stands on g8. Can White save the game by checking again and again?

claims.statement: The engine rates the position as clearly better for Black, depth 16.
A black bishop stands on g8.

hints: Where was the queen checking from before?
Which of those squares is now covered or blocked?
The bishop stands on the last row, next to the king.
items.explain: No. The bishop on g8 gets in the way of the checks along the last row, and the queen has no other series of checks. The chess program rates Black as clearly better, so the draw is not there.

items.prompt: White has a rook and a queen against nothing but pawns. Can White save the game by checking again and again?

claims.statement: Ra8 is checkmate.
A white rook stands on a1.

hints: Is White in danger at all here?
Look for a way to end the game at once.
The rook can go to the last row.
items.explain: Not needed. White is far ahead: the rook goes to a8 and it is checkmate. Asking for a repetition only makes sense when you cannot do better.

items.prompt: White's queen has just checked on e8, and Black's king stepped to h7. White to move: which queen move gives check again?

claims.statement: The queen can go to e4.
After the move the black king on h7 is attacked.
The engine rates the position as level, depth 16.

hints: The king is on h7. Which line could the queen use to attack it?
The queen moves down the e-file.
Queen to e4, which attacks along the diagonal.
items.explain: From e4 the queen attacks the king along the diagonal from e4 to h7. A queen on e5, e6 or e7 does not attack h7, and a queen on h5 is blocked by the pawn on h6.

feedback_by_move.e8h5: The queen on h5 faces the pawn on h6, so the king on h7 is not attacked: no check, and the series of checks ends.

items.prompt: White is a rook ahead and this position has appeared twice, with White to move. What should White play?

claims.statement: White to move wins (tablebase).
The rook can go to a7.

hints: What would the third appearance allow?
Does White have a way to make progress?
One rook move cuts the black king off from the rest of the board.
items.explain: Rook to a7. Another round of shuffling would bring the position up a third time and allow a draw claim. The rook on the seventh row cuts the king off and starts a real plan.

items.prompt: It is Black's turn here. Black is not in check and has no legal move. Does the game end now, without anyone asking for it?

claims.statement: Black is stalemated.

hints: Is the black king in check?
Does Black have any legal move?
Stalemate is one of the draws that happens by itself.
items.explain: Yes. Stalemate ends the game as a draw at once, with no claim needed.

items.prompt: Black's king stepped to d8 and back to e8 while White's king stepped aside and back; both black rooks are home. Black to move. Tap every square Black's king can go to.

claims.statement: The king can go to exactly d7, d8, e7, f7 and f8.
Castling long is not allowed.
Castling short is not allowed.

hints: A king moves one step in any direction.
Empty squares next to the king are open, unless attacked.
Check each of the eight neighbours of e8.
items.explain: Five squares, all next to the king. Both castling moves are gone, because the king itself has moved. The squares look like a fresh start, but the rights are different.

items.prompt: The clock reads 57. White's pawn on e4 takes the pawn on d5. What will the clock read after the move?

claims.statement: The pawn can take on d5.
A black pawn stands on d5.

hints: Look at what moved and whether anything left the board.
Some moves change the game for good.
This one is both a capture and a pawn move.
items.explain: 0. A capture or a pawn move sends the count back to zero, and this move is both.

items.prompt: Position A (Black to move): Black may capture en passant, because White's pawn has just jumped two squares. Position B: the same pieces on the same squares, Black to move, but no pawn has just jumped. Are A and B the same position?

claims.statement: Black may capture en passant.
A white pawn stands on e4.

hints: Compare what Black can legally play in each.
Is there a move that exists in only one of them?
Positions that offer different legal moves are different positions.
items.explain: No. In A Black may capture en passant; in B that move does not exist. Same pieces, same squares, same side to move, but different rights, so different positions.

items.prompt: Black to move, behind in material. Find the move that keeps the game from being lost.

claims.statement: The queen can go to e1.
The engine rates the position as level, depth 16.
After Qe1 the white king on h1 is attacked.

hints: Black cannot win material back. What else can the queen do?
Look at where the white king can run.
Which queen move attacks the king and leaves it few squares?
items.explain: The queen goes to e1 with check and the white king must go to h2. Even if White later blocks with g3, the checks continue. The chess program rates the position as level (depth 16).

items.prompt: White offers Black a draw and Black says no. Is the game drawn?

claims.statement: The game is still going on: no checkmate, no stalemate, no check.
The move is legal here.

hints: Who has to agree?
An offer is only half of an agreement.
The draw needs both players.
items.explain: No. A draw by agreement needs both players to say yes. An offer that is declined changes nothing, and play goes on.
